text:
[Figure, page 3] Fig. 1 TP
The image is a technical line drawing illustrating the proper method for lifting and handling a submersible pump, likely a deep well turbine pump or similar vertical multistage unit. The diagram shows the pump suspended by a lifting sling attached to a hook above.

Key components and features shown:

- **Lifting Sling**: A heavy-duty webbing or chain sling is wrapped around the upper motor housing of the pump. The sling is secured with a metal buckle or clamp, which is highlighted in an inset circle showing a close-up of the fastening mechanism — including a patterned strap (possibly indicating reinforced material) and a metallic clasp with visible rivets or bolts.

- **Pump Assembly**: The main body consists of a cylindrical motor section with cooling fins, mounted on a base frame with support legs. Below the motor is the pump section, featuring a volute casing and discharge flange.

- **Discharge Flange**: Shown in detail via an arrow pointing to the outlet connection. It is a circular flange with bolt holes around its perimeter, designed for piping connections. A flexible hose or pipe is depicted connected to the flange.

- **Mounting/Support Structure**: The pump rests on a rigid frame with vertical supports and horizontal cross-members, suggesting it may be installed within a well casing or mounting bracket.

- **Detail Callouts**: Two circular insets provide magnified views:
  - One focuses on the sling attachment point on the motor housing, showing how the strap is routed and secured.
  - Another highlights the discharge flange and its connection to the piping system.

This figure serves as an instructional guide for safe installation or removal of the pump, emphasizing correct lifting procedures and connection points. No specific model numbers, dimensions, or torque values are visible, but the schematic clearly communicates mechanical relationships and handling requirements.

The image is a technical line drawing from a pump manual, labeled “Fig. 2 TPD,” illustrating the lifting and rigging configuration for a dual-motor pump assembly.

Main components shown:

- Two electric motors mounted side-by-side on a common baseplate or skid.
- A central pump housing (likely a volute casing) with a flanged discharge port facing forward.
- Lifting slings (two straps) attached to lifting lugs on the pump housing and routed upward to a single overhead hook — indicating proper rigging for hoisting the entire unit.
- An inset detail (top right) provides a close-up view of the sling attachment point at the pump’s lifting lug, showing how the sling passes through a loop or eyelet secured by a bolt or pin, ensuring secure load distribution during lifting.
- The baseplate includes mounting feet and possibly anchor points for bolting to a foundation.
- The diagram emphasizes correct lifting procedure: slings are symmetrically arranged to balance the load, and the hook is centered above the center of gravity of the assembly.

No specific part numbers, dimensions, or torque values are visible in this figure. The focus is purely on mechanical handling and safe lifting methodology for the pump-motor assembly. The label “TPD” may refer to a specific model series, drawing revision, or internal document code within the manufacturer’s system.

This diagram is essential for installation personnel to understand how to safely lift and position the pump unit without damaging components or risking injury.

text:
[Figure, page 4] Fig. 5 Use of washers for oval bolt holes
The image is a technical diagram illustrating the correct use of washers when installing a pump using bolts through oval (slotted) holes. It shows two views — one full assembly view and one partial close-up — both highlighting the placement of a washer between the bolt head (or nut) and the mounting surface.

Components labeled:
- “Washer”: A flat, circular component placed under the bolt head or nut to distribute load and prevent damage to the mounting surface. The arrow points to the washer positioned between the bolt and the flange.
- “Installation”: Refers to the upper flange or mounting plate being installed onto the pump.
- “Pump”: The lower component with an irregularly shaped flange that contains the oval bolt holes for alignment or adjustment during installation.

The diagram demonstrates that washers are required on both sides of the flange interface — one under the bolt head (on the installation side) and one under the nut (on the pump side) — to ensure proper clamping force and avoid deformation or stress concentration in the material, especially important when using slotted holes which may allow for positional adjustment.

No specific part numbers, dimensions, or torque values are shown; the focus is purely on the correct mechanical assembly practice for mounting hardware.
